conclusion: Not a misstatement. Control of the products passes to Galah Retail Electronics when its receiving officer signs the delivery docket at the distribution centre (CON-003-T2). The agreement also gives a 30-day return right for unsold products (CON-003-T3) and a 3% volume rebate on annual purchases above AUD 600,000 (CON-003-T4); these affect the amount of revenue, not the transfer point.

reasoning_chain.text: Clause 4.2 (CON-003-T2): title to and risk in the products pass when the customer's receiving officer signs the delivery docket at the distribution centre.
Clause 5.1 (CON-003-T3): the customer may return unsold, undamaged products in original packaging within 30 days after delivery for a full credit.
Clause 6.1 (CON-003-T4): if purchases in a contract year exceed AUD 600,000 net of returns, the supplier pays a rebate of 3% of those purchases.
Revenue is recognised when the customer obtains control of the promised goods (AASB 15 para 31).
For an obligation satisfied at a point in time, indicators of control include legal title, physical possession and the significant risks and rewards of ownership (AASB 15 para 38).
Title, risk and physical possession pass on signature of the delivery docket, so control transfers at that point.
The return right and the volume rebate make the consideration variable but do not change when control passes; revenue is recognised on signature of the delivery docket.

counter_argument: Evidence that the customer can direct the products or that the supplier keeps the risks after the docket is signed, for example a consignment practice, would move the transfer point.
